title: Posters, Glass, and Argument
subtitle: Vesperian society and visual identity
summary: Red, cream and green; iron and glass; walls covered in print, scarves and society pins, machines meant to be beautiful, and arguing in public as a civic duty.
content:
> *"If it works, it can also be beautiful. If it's ugly, explain why."*
> — said in Vesperian workshops

Vesper looks like a country that believes the future is going to be better and intends to argue about the details. Its visual identity is about **movement**, **optimism**, **individuality**, **argument**, **public life** and **technological modernity**. Where Aurelia aims for order and the Vardic Holds for things built to endure, Vesper aims for something that works, looks wonderful and has a political opinion.

This entry describes how the [Vesper Republic](factions.html#vesper-republic) looks and sounds. For its history, see [[the-vesper-republic|The Vesper Republic]]. For the faith whose flame is on every banner, see [[sacred-flame|The Sacred Flame]].

## Colours and Materials

The Vesperian palette is the most colourful of the great powers: **red**, **cream**, **blue**, **gold** and **green**, in painted iron, glass, copper, brass, enamel, textiles and above all **printed paper**.

The Republic's emblem is a **torch** whose flame rises from a sunburst, framed by **laurel** and a ring of **gear teeth**: the Flame, enlightenment and industry in a single device. Flames, rays, laurel and upward-sweeping curves repeat across Vesperian design, on badges, banners, ironwork and the trim of coats.

![The flag of the Vesper Republic](data/images/vesper-republic-flag-dfa78739.jpg "The Vesperian flag: a torch whose flame rises from a sunburst, ringed by laurel and gear teeth, on a cream-and-green cross over deep red, with curving Art Nouveau flourishes in the corners. The same torch appears on civic badges, pins and street banners.")

## Iron, Glass and Boulevards

Vesperian cities are built in **iron** and **glass**, with curved decorative structures, public sculpture, broad boulevards, cafés, tram lines, great railway stations and civic buildings, all of it plastered with posters. Their style is industrial modernity that believes it can be beautiful too. (For players: think **Belle Époque** and **Art Nouveau**.)

![A Vesperian city above its harbour](data/images/vesper-republic-homeland-bdd4f282.jpg "A Vesperian capital in full sun. Notice the iron-and-glass arcades and station roofs, the tram crossing a long viaduct, red torch banners on every public building, domes and towers climbing the hillside, steamers in the harbour, and airships overhead.")

![Another view of a Vesperian city](data/images/vesper-republic-homeland-2-0ac4afd9.jpg "Another Vesperian city: wrought-iron colonnades and torch banners in the foreground, glass-roofed halls by the water, arched viaducts carrying the city over its falls, and airships moving above the hills.")

The intended effect is of a city in motion: things being built, things moving through it, and things being announced on every wall.

## Walls That Talk

**Posters, newspapers, pamphlets and advertisements are everywhere**, and political print is the most important of them. A Vesperian wall is a public forum. On any given street you can find a meeting being advertised, a strike being announced, a politician being attacked, a lecture being promoted, a play being reviewed, a reform being demanded and a new kind of soap being sold, often on top of one another.

The result is a visually noisy public environment that visitors either love or find exhausting, and frequently both by the end of the first day.

> **A print shop in the Old Market district, very late at night**
>
> The press thumped steadily. The printer pulled another sheet, held it up to the lamp and frowned.
>
> "Red's too thin."
>
> Her apprentice looked at the poster. It said, in letters a hand high, **THE TRAM FARE IS A TAX ON THE POOR**.
>
> "It's readable."
>
> "Readable is for the timetable. This is going up opposite the Ministry. They should be able to read it from their windows." She reached for the ink. "And it has to still be red in a week, when they've had time to be angry about it."

Art in Vesper is not something kept in collections. Murals, posters, prints, sculptures, banners, decorative ironwork, advertisements and revolutionary memorials belong in streets, cafés, stations and public buildings, where everyone can see them and argue about them.

## What Vesperians Wear

Vesperian dress allows for personal expression, and Vesperians take advantage of it. Common features are **fitted long coats**, **scarves**, **colourful waistcoats**, **political pins**, **society badges** and individual decoration. Even a uniform rarely stays entirely uniform: a club pin, a union badge, a political ribbon or an artistic flourish usually finds its way on.

![Vesperian clothing: commoner, diplomat, soldier and Expeditioner](data/images/vesper-republic-clothing-e239bbb2.jpg "Four Vesperians. A worker-citizen in a tailored waistcoat with a red scarf, the commonest civic accessory, and notebooks and tools to hand; a republican official in elegant Art Nouveau tailoring with a civic badge; a soldier of the Republic in a service cap bearing its emblem, with brass fittings and practical kit; and a Gate Expeditioner with goggles for fieldwork and Gate phenomena, and pouches of notebooks, maps, instruments and specimen cases.")

- **The scarf** is the closest thing Vesper has to a national garment. It is practical, cheap and endlessly variable, and its colour can say a great deal about its wearer's politics.
- **Pins and badges** show which societies, clubs, unions and causes someone belongs to. Many Vesperians wear several.
- **Officials** dress elegantly, and their civic badge is worn as a pin or used as a seal.
- **Expeditioners** dress practically, and almost always individually. Two Vesperian Expeditioners in identical gear would be a remarkable coincidence.

## Machines Meant to Be Beautiful

Vesperians associate technology with the possibility of a better society, and they want their machines to look like it. A Vesperian engine may be finished in enamel and decorated with curving ironwork, not because the decoration does anything, but because a machine that people will have to live alongside ought to be pleasant to live alongside.

> **At the unveiling of an experimental pumping station, with an Aurelian guest**
>
> The engineer pulled the cloth away with a flourish. The machine underneath was green and gold, with copper flowers climbing its housing.
>
> The Aurelian inspector studied it for some time.
>
> "Has it been tested?"
>
> "It is being tested," said the engineer.
>
> "Now?"
>
> "Since about eight o'clock this morning. It's going very well." She patted the housing. "And before you ask, the flowers are structural. Well. Mostly."

## Arguing in Public

The culturally admired Vesperian is **engaged**, **curious**, **willing to challenge**, **willing to explain why** and **prepared to take part**. A Vesperian does not have to be a radical, a believer or a republican zealot, and most are none of those things. But staying silent in the face of an obviously bad argument can feel to a Vesperian almost like a failure of civic duty.

> **Outside the municipal offices, a queue of twenty people watching**
>
> "The notice says the market permits will be issued *at the discretion* of the district office."
>
> "That is correct, citizen."
>
> "The Charter says municipal decisions affecting trade *shall* be published with reasons. Discretion is not a reason."
>
> "It is the wording we have been given."
>
> "Then I'd like the name of whoever gave it to you, so I can write to them." She turned to the queue. "Does anyone have a pencil?"
>
> Seven people did.

## What Foreigners Get Wrong

Visitors often decide that Vesper is chaotic, that every Vesperian is a revolutionary, and that nothing in the Republic is ever decided. None of this is quite true. The arguments are loud, but the trams run, the courts sit and the Charter is amended through procedure, not riots. Most Vesperians are not extremists. They are simply people who were raised to believe that asking *why* is a citizen's job, and who expect you to have an answer.
